business_ops.supply_chain_integration: Backward integration is centred on in-house fibre regeneration rather than upstream fibre manufacture. The Company imports end-of-life para-aramid fabrics (e.g. expired bulletproof vests) and runs a dedicated regenerating machine for high-strength fibres supporting a proprietary 'Fabric-to-Fibre' recycling process that breaks down and reconstitutes aramid fabrics while retaining tensile strength and thermal resistance; the recycled fibres are fed back as secondary raw material into brake pads, clutch facings, filtration media and protective textiles, reducing dependence on imported virgin fibres and lowering raw material cost. Beyond this, the Company is a single-stage spinner: raw fibre is bought in (polypropylene fibre, high-tenacity polyester, modacrylic fibre, para-aramid fibre, FR viscose fibre and specialised blends such as melamine and peroxidised PAN) and converted through blowroom, carding, drawing, roving, ring frame / DREF friction spinning / open-end spinning, winding, TFO doubling, rewinding and packing, all at the single Petlad unit. Procurement is managed by a Purchase and Supply Chain Department across a mixed domestic and international vendor base with no long-term supply agreements; specialty fibres are largely imported (imports 36.92% of total purchase in FY25) while polypropylene and polyester are domestic. Forward integration is limited - the Company sells B2B into converters and does not process into finished fabrics or garments, though it operates a fabric line within Protech and takes job work where customers supply the raw material (Rs 1,009.09 lakhs, 8.85% of FY25 revenue from operations) and does a small amount of yarn trading (Rs 305.28 lakhs, 2.68%). Energy is partially self-supplied: a 380 KW rooftop solar system at Petlad plus a 4 MW captive solar plant on leased land at Kankanpur, expected to substitute a significant portion of electricity requirements from FY 2025-26. Utilities are otherwise bought in (power from Madhya Gujarat Vij Company Ltd, industrial water by tanker from a local supplier). Manpower as of August 31, 2025 is approximately 156 permanent employees (2 executive directors, 8 finance/accounts/administration, 1 legal and secretarial, 5 technical staff, 2 quality management, 6 sales and marketing, 14 supervisors and in-charges, 118 skilled and unskilled staff), with 119 registered under EPF and no contract labour employed.

market_position.basis: The DRHP does not state any market share for the Company (the only share figures in the industry section are country shares of India's technical-textile import market, e.g. China ~38% in FY 2025). Positioning is inferred from the Company's own description: a single-segment spinner of technical textile yarns at Petlad, Gujarat (para-aramid based spun yarn, high-tenacity polyester, meta-aramid and FR viscose, polypropylene, modacrylic, poly-poly core spun and stainless-steel yarn) serving Indutech, Protech, Mobiltech and Hometech end-uses, with a proprietary 'Fabric-to-Fibre' recycling route for end-of-life para-aramid fabrics. Combined installed capacity 4,775 MT in FY25 (4,525 MT in FY24 and FY23) with 81.68%, 77.10% and 76.82% utilisation; revenue from operations of Rs 11,403.40 lakhs in FY2025 against listed peers of Rs 20,786.87 lakhs (Cedaar Textile) to Rs 4,82,528.78 lakhs (RSWM). Exports were 38.05%, 43.59% and 36.15% of revenue from operations in Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023. The DRHP itself describes the Indian technical textile yarn market as a mix of large integrated manufacturers, mid-sized specialised firms and a broad base of SMEs, with smaller players operating in focused verticals.

opportunities: Production capacity enhancement and cost optimisation within the existing Petlad facility through additional compact spinning systems and high-value attachments such as the Pinter Hard Core system for core-spun and specialty yarns, funded through the proposed capital expenditure under Objects of the Issue.

Expansion of global market reach: the Company proposes to increase installed capacity to service international markets and grow the export share of revenue, having recorded exports of Rs 4,339.15 lakhs, Rs 4,789.49 lakhs and Rs 3,539.55 lakhs (38.05%, 43.59% and 36.15% of revenue from operations) in Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023, and to target additional export markets with demand for specialised technical yarns.

Diversification into high-value technical yarn markets such as milled acrylic and milled carbon yarns for fire-resistant fabrics, composite reinforcement and advanced industrial textiles, described as seeing increased global demand from stricter safety, performance and sustainability requirements.
Automation and digitisation across manufacturing and administrative processes, including integrated planning systems, automated inventory management and data-driven monitoring and analytics.

Import substitution potential: the DRHP notes that high-performance yarns such as aramids and UHMWPE continue to be imported because of the absence of local manufacturing capacity, and that companies developing indigenous substitutes or enhancing yarn properties through blending and finishing are likely to secure a competitive advantage.
Cost reduction from captive renewable power, with the 4 MW solar plant expected to substitute a significant portion of electricity requirements from FY 2025-26 onwards.
strengths: Recycling and sustainable fibre solutions: a dedicated regenerating machine for high-strength fibres supports the Company's proprietary 'Fabric-to-Fibre' process, in which end-of-life imported para-aramid fabrics are broken down and reconstituted while retaining tensile strength and thermal resistance, and the recycled fibre is used in brake pads, clutch facings, filtration media and protective textiles; stated to reduce dependence on imported virgin fibre and lower raw material cost.

Polypropylene spun yarn range manufactured on advanced spinning technologies across a wide range of counts and plies in single and multiple-end formats; PP yarn sales were approximately 22.64%, 21.27% and 26.66% of revenue from operations in Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023.
Three yarn production technologies (Ring Spun, DREF / friction spun and Open-End) across five processing lines, giving flexibility across domestic and international customer requirements.

Long-standing supplier and customer relationships: a significant portion of raw material is procured from the top suppliers and a significant portion of revenue is derived from top customers, which the DRHP describes as delivering a high proportion of repeat business in filtration, automotive friction materials and protective textiles.

Quality control infrastructure including a Mesdan Evenness Tester for yarn uniformity and tensile strength and the Pinter Hard Core attachment system for core and high-torque specialty yarns; defect and rejection rates of 0.40%, 0.03% and 0.13% of revenue from operations in Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023.

ESG and certification profile: ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015, ISO 45001:2018, 5S and OEKO-TEX Standard 100; a 380 KW rooftop solar system at the Petlad unit (connection released by MGVCL on January 19, 2022) and a 4 MW captive solar plant at Village Kankanpur, Godhra (GETCO erection and commissioning certificate February 07, 2025; GEDA commissioning certificate April 30, 2025) expected to substitute a significant portion of electricity requirements from FY 2025-26.
threats: Highly competitive technical textile industry with both organised and unorganised players ranging from small-scale manufacturers to large integrated companies; the DRHP states the Company faces competition from listed peers RSWM Limited, Reliance Chemotex, Garware Technical Fibres Limited and Cedaar Textile Limited (Source: D&B Report), with large enterprises benefiting from scale and wider distribution networks and smaller manufacturers competing on price and flexibility.
Competition from substitute materials and evolving manufacturing processes that may affect demand for existing products.

Protectionist trade measures: on August 27, 2025 the US announced a 50% tariff on most Indian goods imported; the DRHP records that the textile sector is facing order cancellations and that the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry expects a 20-25% reduction in exports to the US over the next six months, against the Company's 38.05% export share of FY2025 revenue from operations.

Dependence on imported specialised fibres (aramids, carbon fibre, PTFE are noted as not domestically produced in India), exposing sourcing to global supplier availability, price movements, currency risk and supply chain disruption.
Peer scale disadvantage on price-based competition: peer revenue from operations for Fiscal 2025 ranges up to Rs 4,82,528.78 lakhs (RSWM Limited) against the Company's Rs 11,403.40 lakhs.

Macroeconomic moderation: global GDP growth projected to slow to 3.0% in CY 2025 from 3.3% in CY 2024, with India's FY26 GDP growth forecast cut to 6.4% on tariff-related uncertainty weighing on exports and investment.
Counterparty credit risk and delays or non-receipt of customer payments, and interest rate increases on the Company's floating-rate borrowings.
weaknesses: No long-term agreements for the supply of raw materials; the Company sources the majority of raw materials from its top 10 suppliers and is dependent on a limited number of customer-approved suppliers for para-aramid fibres.
Customer concentration: top ten customers contributed approximately 67.40%, 72.11% and 68.06% of total income in Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023.

Product and segment concentration: business is heavily dependent on sale of para-aramid based spun yarn and 100% polypropylene spun yarn, and the Company operates in a single business segment (spinning of technical textile yarn).

Single-location operations: all manufacturing is concentrated in one facility at Petlad, Gujarat, and both the registered office and the manufacturing unit operate on leased premises (expansion plans and the renewable energy projects also depend on leased premises).
Capacity under-utilisation: combined utilisation of 81.68%, 77.10% and 76.82% in FY25, FY24 and FY23, with the 100% polypropylene line (up to 2 NE) at 63.75%, 66.38% and 75.34%.
Negative cash flows experienced in the past, flagged as a risk to cash flow requirements and growth plans.

Leverage: debt-equity ratio of 1.60 times as on March 31, 2025 and term loans plus working capital limits of approximately Rs 5,743.50 lakhs, with restrictive covenants under financing agreements, lender charge over movable and immovable properties, and unsecured loans that may be recalled at any time.
B2B model dependent on institutional clients, exposing revenue to any reduction in their demand.
Export obligations under duty exemption schemes and benefits availed under the Advance Authorisation Scheme, with adverse consequences if conditions are not complied with.
Promoters and Directors, other than Independent Directors, do not have prior experience of directorship in a listed company.

overview.business_model: The Company spins specialised yarns (para-aramid, meta-aramid, modacrylic blends, peroxidised PAN, antistatic polypropylene, FR viscose blends, HT polyester, poly-poly corespun and DREF-spun yarns) at its Petlad, Gujarat plant using three technologies - Ring Spun, DREF (friction spun) and Open-End spinning - across five processing lines, and sells them business-to-business as raw-material inputs to industrial manufacturers, processors and institutional buyers in filtration and pollution control, construction/infrastructure, automotive friction materials, packaging (antistatic FIBC), safety and protective equipment, and home furnishing. Products are customised to client technical specifications and supplied on a recurring basis rather than to retail consumers. Revenue is a combination of (i) manufacturing, the principal activity and largest share of revenue in each of the last three financial years, (ii) trading of goods (yarn) and (iii) job-work services where the customer supplies the raw material and the Company converts it into finished yarn. A 380 KW rooftop solar system at Petlad and leased land for a 4 MW solar facility are for captive consumption to lower power cost.

A slowdown in end-use industries (industrial filtration, protective clothing, home textiles), import dependence for para-aramid, meta-aramid, modacrylic and FR viscose, crude-linked petrochemical input pricing, evolving domestic and international regulation, and customer concentration together expose production costs and operating margins. Limited ability to pass on cost increases; failure to innovate or upgrade manufacturing systems could erode competitive position.

strategy_growth.detail: A significant portion of revenue derives from two product lines. Demand and pricing for these yarns are influenced by raw material costs, domestic and international competition, customer preferences and market conditions beyond the Company's control, and there are no long-term agreements with most customers to secure continued order levels.

strategy_growth.detail: All revenues derive from spinning of technical textile yarns including para-aramid based yarns, polypropylene yarns, meta-aramid/viscose blends and other specialty fibres, with no alternate lines of business to mitigate a downturn. Reduced demand, adverse industry trends, increasing competition, regulatory developments, changes in customer preference or pricing pressure would directly hit revenues and profitability, and the concentrated model heightens exposure to raw material cost volatility, specialty fibre supply disruption, technological obsolescence and substitute materials.

strategy_growth.detail: The Company supplies yarns and fabrics to industrial manufacturers, processors and institutional buyers rather than retail consumers, serving filtration and pollution control (filter media, cartridges, cloths), construction and infrastructure (geotextiles, ropes, webbings), automotive (friction materials, thermal insulation, seat fabrics), packaging (antistatic FIBC), safety and protective equipment (flame-retardant clothing, industrial protective wear, PPE kits) and home furnishing (carpets, upholstery, curtains, home filtration media). Revenues depend on customers' procurement cycles and growth; with no long-term purchase commitments, orders are placed on immediate requirements. There is no diversified retail base to offset adverse developments in institutional demand, and B2B competitive pressure may constrain pricing.

concerns_observed: The DRHP itself attributes the FY25 profit step-up to a one-off, not to trading: 'The Company's profit after tax increased by Rs 145.98 lakhs (20.71%) to Rs 850.92 lakhs in Fiscal 2025, compared to Rs 704.94 lakhs in Fiscal 2024, primarily due to an increase in other income', and profit before tax rose Rs 131.55 lakhs 'primarily on account of an increase in other income' - where other income rose Rs 92.26 lakhs from Rs 1.74 lakhs to Rs 94.00 lakhs and the MD&A states the increase 'is mainly due to sale of property, plant and equipment'.

No vendor order behind the capital-expenditure object: 'We have considered the above quotations for the budgetary estimate purpose and have not placed orders for them. No orders have been placed with any of the aforementioned vendors.' All 21 civil and machinery line items behind the Rs 2,495.75 lakhs object rest on budgetary quotations, and several lapse before deployment - Vandewiele Savio cone winders February 7, 2026 and two-for-one twisters February 09, 2026, Parmeshwar Construction civil works February 25, 2026, Adishwar Electricals February 26, 2026, with LMW Limited valid only 'until 45 days from the date of the Issue'. The Savio quotations were struck in Euros at 1 EUR = Rs 103.15 as on August 22, 2025.

The finance function turned over twice within six weeks of filing: a Chief Financial Officer, Dhyan Narendra Vyas, was appointed with effect from September 01, 2025 and resigned with effect from September 05, 2025 'due to pre-occupation' - four days - with Alpesh Rameshchandra Bhavsar appointed September 11, 2025 and the Company Secretary and Compliance Officer appointed August 01, 2025. All three Independent Directors were appointed on July 14, 2025 and the Audit, Nomination and Remuneration and Stakeholders Relationship Committees were constituted on August 01, 2025, so no committee has a track record predating the filing.

A long RoC non-compliance record disclosed by the Company: delays in annual filings (AOC-4, MGT-7, 23AC/23ACA) of up to 128 days for FY 2021-22 and FY 2023-24; delays of 7 to 264 days in Form-32 / DIR-12 filings for director appointments, resignations and designation changes; an adjudication application filed with the RoC for incorrect related-party disclosure in Form AOC-4 for FY 2022-23; and Form CHG-1 never filed for creation of charge on car loans from BMW India Financial Services Private Limited and ICICI Bank, which the DRHP states is non-compliance with Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 and may attract penalties under Section 86.

Provident Fund contributions were not deducted on salary paid to Promoter(s), Directors and Key Managerial Personnel, which the Company states constitutes non-compliance with applicable PF regulations; 119 of the approximately 156 permanent employees were registered with EPF as of August 31, 2025, with Rs 3.25 lakhs deposited with the EPFO for August 2025. No penalties have been levied as at the DRHP date and no assurance is given against future audits or punitive action.

Leverage rose materially into the filing: total borrowings of Rs 3,045.12 lakhs (FY23), Rs 3,486.32 lakhs (FY24) and Rs 5,743.50 lakhs (FY25) against net worth of Rs 2,071.45 / 2,755.39 / 3,585.31 lakhs, taking the printed debt-equity ratio to 1.60 times as on March 31, 2025 from 1.27 times a year earlier; finance costs Rs 307.02 / 332.44 / 407.70 lakhs. Secured outstanding debt was Rs 3,651.53 lakhs at March 31, 2025 and all 12 secured facilities are floating-rate, with lenders holding a charge over movable and immovable properties.

The unsecured funding leg is entirely a related-party dependency with no amortisation schedule: outstanding unsecured loans of Rs 2,091.97 lakhs as of March 31, 2025 comprised Rs 2,091.97 lakhs from related parties and Rs 0.00 lakhs from others, of which Rs 1,336.98 lakhs is repayable on demand and Rs 755.00 lakhs after 6 years. The loan table prints a fixed 12.00% on every unsecured related-party line - Prahash Fin-Stock, Abhishek R. Agarwal, Siddharth P. Patel, Binaben P. Patel, Nishtha Agarwal, Shilpa Abhishek Agarwal, Shradha Sankit Agarwal and others - while the risk factor describes the range as 10% to 12% per annum.

Related-party transactions run at Rs 1,819.33 lakhs (18.58% of revenue from operations) in FY23, Rs 1,768.60 lakhs (16.10%) in FY24 and Rs 2,080.85 lakhs (18.25%) in FY25, and both premises are rented from related entities: the sole Petlad manufacturing facility is leased from group company Shyamprakash Spinning Mills Limited, in which promoter Siddharth Patel holds a 6.11% equity stake, at Rs 75,000 per month to March 31, 2033; the registered office is leased from Pitex Corporation, in which Anar Patel, wife of promoter Siddharth Patel, holds a 25% partnership interest, at Rs 5,000 per month to October 31, 2027.

Concentration on both sides of the book with no long-term contracts on either: top 10 customers were 68.06% / 72.11% / 67.40% of revenue from operations in FY23 / FY24 / FY25 and the single largest 16.05% / 25.53% / 19.75%; top 10 suppliers were 82.45% / 78.10% / 70.31% of raw-material purchases and the largest 20.11% / 14.69% / 13.19%. Imports were 38.52% / 41.18% / 36.92% of total purchase, and customers mandate that para-aramid, viscose and acrylic fibres be procured only from their own pre-approved suppliers, so the Company cannot switch vendors without customer approval.

Single facility, single segment, two dominant products: all manufacturing is at one leased unit at Petlad, Gujarat under a 10-year lease running April 01, 2023 to March 31, 2033; the Company operates in one business segment (technical textile yarn spinning); and para-aramid based spun yarn (23.87% of FY25 revenue from operations) plus 100% polypropylene yarn (22.64%) carry the mix. Gujarat alone was 29.67% of FY25 revenue from operations and 40.05% of raw-material purchases.

Cash generation has not kept pace with the investment programme: cash from operations of Rs 1,212.07 / 563.54 / 1,122.22 lakhs against capital expenditure of Rs 285.73 / 906.93 / 2,822.64 lakhs (2.92% / 8.25% / 24.75% of revenue from operations) for FY23 / FY24 / FY25; FY25 investing outflow of Rs (2,629.91) lakhs was met by financing inflow of Rs 1,828.50 lakhs including Rs 3,497.95 lakhs of long-term borrowing proceeds. Net working capital rose to Rs 3,659.60 lakhs, 32.09% of revenue from operations, from 22.95% in FY23, and net capital turnover fell from 14.70 to 14.56 to 9.47 times while inventory turnover fell from 10.87 to 10.21 to 8.41 times. The DRHP prints these as turnover ratios in times and prints no debtor, inventory, creditor or cash-conversion days anywhere.

The capital structure was rebuilt in the weeks before filing: authorised equity capital was raised from Rs 175.00 lakhs to Rs 2,500.00 lakhs at the EGM of July 23, 2025, and an 8:1 bonus was allotted on September 15, 2025 out of Reserves & Surplus - 14 days before this DRHP dated September 29, 2025 - lifting the share count from 17,50,000 to 1,57,50,000 and paid-up capital from Rs 175.00 lakhs to Rs 1,575.00 lakhs. The Securities Premium Account before the Issue is nil because every allotment since 1985 was at face value of Rs 1,000 per share.

Promoters' certified entry cost sits far below book: statutory-auditor-certified weighted average cost of acquisition of Rs 0.72 per share for Siddharth Prakash Patel (12,71,700 shares), Rs 1.59 for Prahash Fin-stock Private Limited (27,45,900 shares) and Rs 2.06 for Abhishek Rajendrakumar Agarwal (23,40,000 shares), against a post-bonus adjusted NAV per Equity Share of Rs 22.76 as on March 31, 2025 and an Issue Price printed as [BLANK]. The DRHP carries its own risk factor 45 on this point. Two secondary transactions in the preceding three years were both gifts on August 20, 2024 at nil consideration.

The register is thin and locks up entirely: only 15 shareholders on the date of filing, of whom 13 hold 1.00% or more, together 1,56,81,384 shares or 99.55%. All pre-issue Equity Shares are to be locked in before listing - 20% of post-issue capital as minimum promoters' contribution for 3 years, the promoter excess 50% for 1 year and 50% for 2 years, and all other pre-issue holdings including the bonus shares for 1 year - so free float at listing is the Issue itself. Promoters alone hold 63,57,600 shares (40.37%) and Promoter plus Promoter Group 94,17,600 shares (59.79%).

Litigation and statutory obligations, taken direction by direction as the DRHP prints them: against the Company, 12 tax matters aggregating Rs 254 lakhs (TDS/TCS 9 cases Rs 0.16 lakhs; GST 3 cases Rs 253.84 lakhs); against the Promoters, 2 tax matters aggregating Rs 2.63 lakhs; against the Group Company, 4 tax matters aggregating Rs 158.21 lakhs; and one matter filed by the Group Company, Special Civil Application No. 15830 of 2010 before the Gujarat High Court, for Rs 671.52 lakhs. Directors and KMP/Senior Management are nil in both directions. Separately, obligation to export against import stood at Rs 285.06 / 343.53 / 535.82 lakhs for FY23 / FY24 / FY25, with bank guarantees of Rs 59.35 / 59.35 / 99.35 lakhs.

Governance and disclosure hygiene gaps beyond the RoC record: the Company states 'we have not adopted any formal code of conduct'; it has not obtained a credit rating in the last three Fiscals; the logo trademark application is only at 'formalities check pass' so no statutory protection exists; and Promoters and Directors other than the Independent Directors have no prior experience of directorship in a listed company. The PCS ROC report dated September 29, 2025 flags that the increase in authorised capital from Rs 10.00 lakhs to Rs 30.00 lakhs and the ROC form for the September 28, 1985 issue of 2,398 shares are not traceable, with reliance placed on Company minutes dated September 27, 1985.

The second production line is going backwards while the first tightens: 100% polypropylene yarn (up to 2 NE) utilisation fell from 75.34% (FY23) to 66.38% (FY24) to 63.75% (FY25) on a flat installed 1,025 MT, with actual production down from 772 MT to 680 MT to 653 MT, even as the proposed expansion adds 1,250 MTPA of synthetic yarn from 22 to 50 NE.

Export exposure meets a live tariff shock: the DRHP records the United States announcement of August 27, 2025 imposing a 50% tariff on most Indian goods, states that the textile sector is facing order cancellations, and cites the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry expecting a 20-25% reduction in exports to the US over the following six months - against exports of 38.05% of FY25 revenue from operations and reciprocal tariffs of 10% to 50% affecting both export sales and US-sourced specialty fibre.

Neither the amount nor the destination of a large part of the proceeds is fixed: the General Corporate Purposes amount is printed as [BLANK], capped at 15% of Gross Proceeds or Rs 1,000.00 lakhs whichever is lower; the specific borrowings to be repaid from the Rs 2,500.00 lakhs object are not identified and selection is left to stated commercial factors; prepayment penalty on the Citibank term loans is 2% of sanction amount or principal outstanding, whichever is higher, at Citibank's discretion; and the fund requirements have not been appraised by any bank, financial institution or independent agency, with no alternate source of financing identified.

Insurance cover as a proportion of assets has fallen sharply as the asset base grew: insured property, plant and equipment excluding land was 93.89% of PPE-except-land at March 31, 2023 and 90.82% at March 31, 2024, but only 73.40% (Rs 5,942.17 lakhs) at March 31, 2025, in a single-site operation where a fire or breakdown has no alternate facility to absorb it. Inventories remain 100% insured in all three years.

The litigation total of Rs 1,086.36 lakhs and the derived 127.67% of profit after tax and 30.30% of net worth carried in the assembled inputs add matters filed BY parties to matters filed AGAINST them and add across four different party categories. The DRHP prints no aggregate total for contingent liabilities, commitments and obligations - only the line items bank guarantee Rs 99.35 lakhs, obligation to export against import Rs 535.82 lakhs and capital-account commitments Rs 87.23 lakhs for FY2024-25 (advance paid Rs 21.00 lakhs). Financial information for the three group companies - Shree Prakash Textiles (Gujarat) Private Limited, Shyamprakash Spinning Mills Limited and Shri Bajrangbali Intermediate and Dyechem Private Limited - is not set out in the DRHP; reserves, sales, profit after tax, EPS and NAV for the past three years are referred only to the Company's website. The Company's own market share is not stated anywhere; the only share figures in the industry section are country shares of India's technical-textile import market. Positioning against RSWM, Reliance Chemotex, Garware Technical Fibres and Cedaar Textile rests on the DRHP's peer table alone.

Auditors' qualifications are affirmatively nil, and the litigation tables record no criminal proceedings, no material civil litigation, no statutory or regulatory proceedings and no SEBI or stock-exchange disciplinary action in the last five financial years against the Company, Promoters, Directors or KMP/Senior Management; every disclosed matter against the Company and the Promoters is a tax matter.

Captive power is built and commissioned rather than promised: a 380 KW rooftop solar system at Petlad (MGVCL connection released January 19, 2022) plus a 4 MW ground-mounted captive solar plant on leased Kankanpur land, with GETCO erection and commissioning certificate dated February 07, 2025 and GEDA commissioning certificate dated April 30, 2025, expected to substitute a significant portion of electricity requirements from FY 2025-26.

Established export franchise with third-party certification: exports of Rs 3,539.55 / 4,789.49 / 4,339.15 lakhs, being 36.15% / 43.59% / 38.05% of revenue from operations in FY23 / FY24 / FY25 across China, Germany, Hungary, Brazil, Russia and Italy; ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015, ISO 45001:2018, 5S and OEKO-TEX Standard 100 held; SRTEPC award for Outstanding Export Performance in Specialty Yarns for 2022-23.

A differentiated input route in a business that imports 36.92% of total purchases (FY25): a dedicated regenerating machine supports a proprietary 'Fabric-to-Fibre' process that breaks down end-of-life imported para-aramid fabrics and feeds reconstituted fibre back into brake pads, clutch facings, filtration media and protective textiles, stated to lower dependence on imported virgin fibre.

Product mix is shifting toward the higher-specification end within the existing plant: Meta Aramid / Viscose / Para-aramid based spun yarn rose from 4.50% (FY23) and 3.69% (FY24) to 12.64% of revenue from operations (FY25), Rs 440.25 / 405.72 / 1,441.28 lakhs, and milled aramid from 2.08% to 5.46%.

No ESOP/ESPS/SAR scheme, no outstanding convertible instruments, warrants or depository receipts, and no promoter shares pledged or otherwise encumbered as on the date of the DRHP - Table I of the shareholding pattern shows nil pledged for both Promoter and Promoter Group.
